title: Alypius at the games (Confessions 6.8)
hook: a friend dragged to the gladiators opens his eyes just once and is hooked
tomorrow: what kind of story makes you ashamed you're still stuck?

segments.voice: Augustine's friend died, and everything he looked at was death. Your line: I became a question. Today, another friend, and a different kind of danger.

Everyone at school is passing around the same video, and somebody says: just watch it once, it's nothing. Augustine tells of a friend, Alypius, studying law in Rome. Fellow students coming from dinner drag him, with friendly force, to the gladiator games, which he hates. You can drag my body there, he tells them, but you can't make my mind and eyes look. I'll be absent while present. He sits down and shuts his eyes. And here's the strange part: his eyes are closed, and he still gets hooked. How?
screen: `JUST WATCH IT ONCE.` → `ABSENT WHILE PRESENT.` → `EYES SHUT, AND STILL HOOKED?`

segments.voice: A fighter falls, and a roar goes up from the whole crowd. The sound gets in where his eyes wouldn't. Curiosity wins, and he opens them, sure he can look and stay above it all. Augustine says he took a deeper wound in his soul than the gladiator took in his body. He didn't turn away. He fixed his eyes and drank it in, and in a moment he wasn't the man who came in. He was one of the crowd, shouting, and he carried home a madness that drove him back again, soon bringing others with him. Now the answer to the puzzle, and it's the surprise to pass on. The problem, Augustine says, wasn't that Alypius was weak. It was that he was sure he was strong. He trusted himself and not God, so eyes closed by willpower opened at the first loud noise. The chapter doesn't end in the stadium. Augustine adds that God later pulled Alypius out, and taught him to put his trust somewhere other than himself. That took time. One look was quick.
screen: `EYES SHUT BY WILLPOWER.` · `A ROAR GETS IN.` · `SURE HE WAS STRONG.` · `PULLED OUT, IN TIME.` · then, large: `JUST ONE LOOK.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes for the sit, and notice how often they want to open: a sound, an itch, a thought of your phone. Each time, don't fight it with grit; just notice the pull, and rest again. If you pray, a psalm line fits here: "turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity."
Alypius at the games. Augustine's friend who shut his eyes in the arena, opened them once, and was hooked.
Remember this: just one look, and feeling sure of yourself is the open door. Sleep well.

howItsDone: Christians speak of guarding the eyes and the heart, and some pray Psalm 119:37 when they want to look away from what pulls them; Augustine's chapter is read as a warning about overconfidence.

fork.setup: your friend stays in a group chat that roasts people, sure she can just read it and never join in. what does Alypius's story warn?
options: she's right: knowing the risk is enough to keep her safe.
being sure she's strong is the very door it comes in by.
she should stay and argue with everyone in the chat.
fork.reveal: Alypius shut his eyes and trusted himself; one roar opened them. Augustine says the trust in himself was the trouble.
